title: AI at Two Speeds
description: The AI frontier changes through releases. Society absorbs change through learning, institutions and consent. What happens when those clocks fall out of step?
body:
*Sebastian Mertens · 2 October 2026*

An AI release can change what a builder is willing to attempt before a school has agreed how to assess work produced with the previous generation. A company can still be establishing rules for a writing assistant when its most intensive users begin delegating multi-step tasks. These are illustrative situations, but they expose a question that adoption numbers alone cannot answer: what happens when technical possibility changes faster than people can make it part of ordinary life?

The frontier and society do not run on the same clock. One advances through models, tools and new combinations of them. The other advances through accumulated experience, redesigned work, institutional decisions and negotiated acceptance. Neither is a single process. But a release can arrive without waiting for the learning and decisions prompted by the last one to finish.

**The social risk is not simply that some people have yet to use AI. It is that the terms of participation can change while they are still learning how to participate.** People close to the frontier can help define the next set of expectations; others may be judged against those expectations before they have the conditions to meet them.

This is where agency matters. The mismatch in pace can separate people who use AI to change their circumstances from people whose circumstances are changed by others' deployments. That is a mechanism to investigate, not a measured global lag. The evidence shows substantial capability gains, rapid but uneven diffusion and real constraints on turning tools into useful work. It does not establish a continuously widening aggregate distance between “AI” and “society.”

## Access is only the first threshold

I would separate six questions that the word *adoption* tends to hide.

Technical capability asks what a system can accomplish under specified conditions. Access asks who can obtain the relevant model, tools and infrastructure. Use asks whether people actually employ them, and how often. Productive deployment asks whether the complete activity improves after checking, correction and integration are counted. Organizational change asks whether roles, processes and resources change around that deployment. Social legitimacy asks whether the arrangement is acceptable to the people affected by it.

These are not compulsory stages on a ladder. A useful private application may require no organizational redesign. An institution can grant permission without establishing usefulness. Legitimacy can be lost after a technically successful deployment. It is not a final certification that arrives automatically when enough people subscribe.

This also changes who counts as being near the frontier. Silicon Valley contains researchers, infrastructure workers, cautious enterprise buyers, enthusiasts and people worried about the consequences of their own industry. Outside it, builders can work with advanced agents without belonging to a frontier laboratory. Geography matters, but it is not the definition.

For this argument, proximity means having the tools, practical knowledge, usable context and discretion to attempt consequential work with AI. A premium account helps with only part of that. Time to learn, permission to connect systems and the ability to recover from a failed experiment can matter just as much.

## The frontier has moved, on a measure we can inspect

METR's task-completion time horizon supplies direct evidence of forward movement. It estimates the duration of a human task at which an agent reaches a specified success probability. On its current TH1.1 series, the 50% estimate for GPT-4, released in March 2023, is about four minutes. Claude 3.7 Sonnet, released in February 2025, reaches about an hour; Claude Opus 4.6, released in February 2026, about twelve hours. These are estimates from task evaluations, not descriptions of how long a model can safely work unsupervised. [METR's structured results](https://metr.org/assets/benchmark_results_1_1.yaml)

![METR TH1.1 estimates rise from minutes for models released in 2023 to hours for models released in 2025 and early 2026. Twenty-two estimates below the sixteen-hour reliability boundary are plotted by model release date with 95% confidence intervals on a logarithmic human-task-duration axis.](/images/research/ai-at-two-speeds/01-frontier-time-horizons.svg)

*Figure 1. Historical capability estimates, not a forecast. METR TH1.1, 50% task-success threshold; dots and 95% bootstrap intervals, plotted by model release date. All 22 TH1.1 estimates below 16 hours in the retrieved file are shown. The April 2026 Claude Mythos Preview (early) estimate is omitted because it exceeds METR's stated reliable range. Source: [structured data](https://metr.org/assets/benchmark_results_1_1.yaml) and [methodology/change log](https://metr.org/time-horizons/), retrieved October 2, 2026. No adoption measure shares this axis.*

The uncertainty is material. Opus 4.6's interval spans roughly five to sixty-one hours. METR warns that estimates above sixteen hours are unreliable with this task suite. Its latest listed addition is the early Mythos Preview evaluation, added in May; the file is not a complete census of every model available in October. Release dates on the horizontal axis are not evaluation dates, and earlier models have been retrospectively re-estimated. [TH1.1 methodology](https://metr.org/blog/2026-1-29-time-horizon-1-1/)

The defensible conclusion is substantial improvement across these evaluated generations, not that every release improves performance or that a fitted curve measures general intelligence. Tasks concentrate in software engineering, machine learning and cybersecurity. Scaffolds matter, and most of the suite's longer human baselines are estimated rather than directly timed. Nevertheless, movement from minute-scale to hour-scale tasks is a concrete reason that a builder's assumptions about delegation may need revisiting. Whether that translates into useful work elsewhere is a separate question.

## Society is not standing still

The simplest version of an adoption-gap story is already contradicted by the data.

In Gallup's May 6–20, 2026 survey, 52% of U.S. employees reported using AI in their role at least a few times a year. Thirty percent used it a few times a week or more; 15% used it daily. These are overlapping thresholds among employees, not shares of businesses or measures of autonomous-agent use. The survey covered 22,573 employed adults. [Gallup's July 2026 workplace release](https://www.gallup.com/workplace/712736/organizational-adoption-jumps-six-points.aspx)

![Horizontal bars show that 52% of U.S. employees used AI at work at least a few times a year, 30% at least a few times a week and 15% daily, in May 2026. The categories overlap.](/images/research/ai-at-two-speeds/02-workplace-use.svg)

*Figure 2. Reach is not intensity. Percentage of U.S. employees, May 6–20, 2026. Daily users are included in frequent users, who are included in total users. Source: [Gallup](https://www.gallup.com/workplace/712736/organizational-adoption-jumps-six-points.aspx), published July 20, 2026.*

Gallup also found that 47% of employees said their organization had integrated AI tools, up from 41% in the previous quarter. That is important counterevidence: organizations are moving too. But an employee's report about their employer is not a firm-weighted adoption rate, and neither answer establishes a measured productivity improvement.

The latest U.S. Census Bureau release available for this essay provides a different view. Its September 24 Business Trends and Outlook Survey reports 23.8% of nonfarm employer businesses using AI in any business function. The collection period was September 7–20; the workbook assigns August 24–September 6 as the reference period. The question asks about the last two weeks. This is a business share, covering AI broadly, not generative AI specifically. Census changed the wording in November 2025, so I would not join it to the older question as an uninterrupted series. [Census national workbook](https://www.census.gov/hfp/btos/downloads/National.xlsx); [question-change explanation](https://www.census.gov/library/stories/2026/05/ai-use-businesses.html)

Europe offers another reminder to read the denominator. Eurostat reported that 32.7% of EU residents aged 16–74 used generative AI in the three months before their 2025 survey. The corresponding work-purpose figure was 15.1% of that population, not 15.1% of workers. These figures cannot be ranked directly against Gallup's U.S. employee results: the populations, periods and definitions differ. [Eurostat's December 2025 release](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-eurostat-news/w/ddn-20251216-3)

There is broad diffusion, not a small technical priesthood facing an untouched public. What remains unresolved is how much that reach changes people's practical options.

## Two clocks, and a moving target

The first clock changes the set of plausible actions. A model improvement can make a previously impractical task worth attempting. An interface can make an existing capability easier to use. A builder with appropriate tools and discretion can test that possibility immediately, although many attempts will fail or add little value.

The second clock changes what people can reliably do together. Practical knowledge has to accumulate: where does the tool help, what must be checked, and which exceptions matter? Organizations must make information usable, allocate responsibility and redesign handoffs. Schools and governments also have to decide what is legitimate, not merely executable. Those decisions involve people who did not choose the technology and cannot be treated as test users who are free to leave.

Brynjolfsson, Rock and Syverson's *Productivity J-Curve* explains why general-purpose technologies require complementary investments in processes, human capital and business models. These investments take resources before their benefits become visible. The paper supplies a mechanism for delayed absorption, not a timetable for AI or proof that every unsuccessful project will eventually pay off. [Research paper, published in 2021](https://www.nber.org/papers/w25148)

Repeated frontier changes can complicate that accumulation. Consider an institution validating an assistant that proposes text for a person to approve. If a newer system can also execute operations, the previous work is not worthless, but questions about permissions, supervision and recovery must be reopened. Training for reviewing an answer does not automatically prepare someone to oversee actions. This is a hypothetical example of the moving-target mechanism, not a measured frequency of institutional restarts.

Some learning transfers, and better systems may remove earlier integration costs. The risk arises when material changes arrive before a deployment's users, operating practices and accountability arrangements have stabilized. Attention is diverted from absorbing one possibility to evaluating the next. A group able to experiment continuously may move forward while another is still making its earlier choice dependable. The gap need not widen forever to be socially consequential during that interval.

There is a striking small-scale example of adaptation outrunning the way it is measured. METR's randomized developer study found early-2025 tools increased completion time by 19% in its setting. By its February 2026 follow-up, some developers did not want to participate without AI, and some withheld tasks they particularly wanted to do with it. Newer estimates leaned toward speedup, but selection and concurrent-agent time accounting compromised the comparison. This is evidence that practices changed enough to disrupt the study design, not proof of a universal productivity jump. [Original field experiment](https://metr.org/blog/2025-07-10-early-2025-ai-experienced-os-dev-study/); [2026 follow-up](https://metr.org/blog/2026-02-24-uplift-update/)

There is a revealing result closer to the present. In the September 2026 revision of *Writing Code vs. Shipping Code*, Demirer, Musolff and Yang estimate large increases in coding activity across successive generations of tools, but much smaller increases in releases. Their cumulative estimate reaches 240% for commits and 30% for releases. These are matched observational event-study estimates, not randomized effects or interchangeable measures of useful output. [NBER working paper and revised manuscript](https://www.nber.org/papers/w35275)

The magnitude needs caution; the distinction deserves attention. Producing more intermediate work does not remove every constraint on delivering something people can use. Even near the frontier, checking, coordination and demand remain part of the system.

## Who can afford the transition?

The burden is not simply learning a tool once. It is maintaining the capacity to reconsider what is possible while still delivering the work people depend on. Existing responsibilities do not disappear during the transition.

The capacity to make those investments is uneven. Eurostat's 2025 enterprise survey found AI use in 17.0% of small enterprises, 30.36% of medium enterprises and 55.03% of large enterprises. “Small” here means 10–49 employees and self-employed persons; businesses below ten are outside the survey's coverage. The measure includes multiple AI technologies, not just generative models. [Eurostat enterprise results and scope](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Use_of_artificial_intelligence_in_enterprises)

![AI use among EU enterprises in 2025 was 17.0% for small enterprises with 10–49 persons, 30.4% for medium enterprises with 50–249 persons and 55.0% for large enterprises with at least 250 persons. Firms below ten persons are excluded.](/images/research/ai-at-two-speeds/03-enterprise-size.svg)

*Figure 3. Unequal uptake within the same survey. Percentage of EU enterprises in covered sectors using at least one AI technology, 2025; values rounded to one decimal. Size counts employees and self-employed persons. Source: [Eurostat workbook, Figure 1](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/images/b/bf/2025_Enterprises_using_AI_tables_and_graphs.xlsx), December 2025 extraction.*

Firm size alone does not explain this pattern. Sector, task mix and existing digital capacity also differ. Nor does a large company's adoption mean that every employee benefits. The result nevertheless makes a frictionless account of diffusion difficult to sustain: access to a broadly available technology is compatible with strongly unequal uptake.

The individual distribution is uneven as well. In Eurostat's 2025 data, recent generative-AI use was 49% among people with high formal education and 22% among those with low or no formal education. These are rounded population-group shares, not a test of ability or willingness to learn. [Eurostat's population analysis](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Use_of_artificial_intelligence_by_individuals)

My concern is a reinforcing mechanism, not a causal result extracted from these percentages. People with useful tasks, discretion and support can experiment, learn what works and use the resulting capacity to attempt more. People without those conditions may experience the same period mainly as new expectations. The cost of learning falls on them before any benefit is secure.

That can divide colleagues doing similar work, not just countries or industries. Bick and colleagues' August 2026 working paper, based on U.S. surveys through May, finds substantial variation in adoption within occupations and tasks. Occupational exposure is therefore an incomplete description of who is actually using the technology. [*What Work Does Generative AI Do?*](https://www.nber.org/papers/w35677)

## The strongest objection: AI can close gaps

There is a serious alternative to the story of cumulative advantage. AI can make expertise more accessible. A person need not become a programmer before obtaining help with code, or master professional prose before producing a useful first draft. Better interfaces and integration may remove precisely the barriers that currently favor intensive users.

A randomized online experiment in Argentina gives this argument substance. Cruces and colleagues studied 1,174 adults aged 25–45 completing a business problem-solving task, with or without an AI assistant. In the May 2026 revision, the performance gap between the study's higher- and lower-education groups fell from 0.548 standard deviations without AI to 0.139 with it. That is roughly three-quarters of the initial gap closed. [Experiment, conducted September–November 2025](https://www.nber.org/papers/w34851)

This was an incentivized, bounded task with a supplied assistant and tutorial, not an estimate of wage convergence or economy-wide productivity. Participants needed a computer to take part. Those qualifications do not cancel the finding. They identify conditions under which people with less formal education gained more.

There is related evidence from actual work. Brynjolfsson, Li and Raymond's 2025 journal article studies a staggered rollout to customer-support agents, primarily in autumn 2020 and winter 2021. It estimates a 15% average increase in issues resolved per hour, with larger gains for less experienced and lower-skilled workers. This is a historical field deployment, analyzed using rollout comparisons rather than a randomized trial of the full sample. It demonstrates a possible equalizing mechanism, not the effect of today's tools everywhere. [Published study, author's copy](https://danielle.li/assets/docs/GenerativeAIatWork.pdf)

The implication is uncomfortable for a deterministic inequality thesis: AI can equalize task performance while access to the circumstances that enable that equalization remains unequal. The outcome depends partly on how deployment is organized. A tool provided with paid learning time and useful context is a different intervention from telling employees to improve their productivity in their spare time.

Nor should non-use automatically be classified as deprivation. Some tasks do not benefit enough to justify the cost. Some people reasonably prefer another way of working. A society in which everyone uses AI daily is not necessarily better than one in which people can choose effective tools and refuse unsuitable ones.

I would abandon the stronger “widening gap” claim if repeated evidence showed less advantaged groups obtaining comparable practical gains, institutions sharing those gains and affected people acquiring more influence over deployment. Rising adoption is evidence in that direction, but it does not answer all three questions.

## Use is not consent

The social divide becomes clearer when the question shifts from “Can you use it?” to “Who decides what it does to you?”

An employee might welcome help drafting a report and oppose using the same technology to intensify monitoring. A student might value an explanation and question an assessment system they cannot challenge. A citizen might welcome faster administration and still require a human route to correct a consequential mistake. These are illustrative distinctions, not reports of particular deployments. There is no contradiction in wanting assistance while resisting a transfer of authority.

Pew's June 22–28, 2026 U.S. survey, published in September, found 52% of adults more concerned than excited about AI's increased use in daily life, 37% equally concerned and excited, and 9% more excited than concerned. This is a question about attitudes, not a measure of technical literacy, opposition to every application or direct trust in a particular system. [Pew's September 16 analysis](https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2026/09/16/democrats-are-now-more-worried-than-republicans-about-ai-and-its-impact-on-jobs/)

![In June 2026, 52% of U.S. adults were more concerned than excited about AI in daily life, 37% equally concerned and excited, and 9% more excited than concerned. Bars use a zero-to-100-percent scale.](/images/research/ai-at-two-speeds/04-public-attitudes.svg)

*Figure 4. Concern coexists with diffusion. Percentage of U.S. adults, June 22–28, 2026; sample of 3,488. No-answer responses are omitted and percentages are rounded. Source: [Pew Research Center](https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2026/09/16/democrats-are-now-more-worried-than-republicans-about-ai-and-its-impact-on-jobs/), September 16, 2026. This is a different population from Figure 2, not an adoption-versus-trust time series.*

The same survey found that 71% expected AI to lead to fewer U.S. jobs over the next twenty years. That is an expectation, not a labor-market forecast. It still matters politically: people evaluate the transition partly through the future they believe is being prepared for them.

There is no single global public mood. Pew's September 17 international report finds mixed concern and excitement common across its surveyed countries. Greater awareness can coexist with greater optimism about AI overall and greater concern about jobs. Becoming informed does not force people toward one approved attitude. [Pew's international findings](https://www.pewresearch.org/global/2026/09/17/globally-more-people-expect-ai-to-cause-job-loss-than-growth/)

The two clocks can leave people occupying different practical technological presents. One person's normal workflow includes delegation that another has never been permitted to attempt. One is revising expectations after a successful experiment; another is still accountable for failures in the old process. This interpretation fits the evidence of uneven use and changing practice, but no survey here measures those “presents” as a single distance.

That difference can become power. People able to demonstrate new possibilities may set deadlines, staffing assumptions and definitions of competence for others. An intensive user can read hesitation as ignorance; someone facing an imposed change can read enthusiasm as indifference. Both may be describing their situation accurately. Faster technical learning does not give one group exclusive authority to decide what everyone else should accept.

The frontier's most persuasive demonstration is often an expanded range of things one person can accomplish. The public's most consequential question may be whether that expansion gives their employer, supplier or government more power over them. A better demo does not settle that disagreement.

## Build the capacity to absorb change

The answer is not to demand that every institution copy a frontier lab's release rhythm. I would judge progress by whether people can absorb useful changes without continually losing their footing. That requires capacity for learning and revision, alongside the right not to adopt something merely because it is new.

For work, that means making time for learning part of the transition rather than treating it as an unpaid obligation. It means giving employees a say in what gets automated and making the distribution of gains explicit. An efficiency improvement can support better service, shorter hours, higher output or reduced staffing. The technology does not choose fairly among those outcomes.

For schools, it means preserving the ability to learn and demonstrate understanding while deciding where assistance belongs. A completed assignment and an acquired skill are different outcomes. Students and teachers need usable rules and ways to question them, not a requirement to track every model release before participating in the debate.

For public institutions, it means retaining an accountable route through consequential decisions. People should be able to understand when AI is involved, correct relevant information and reach someone with authority to reconsider the result. Faster processing can be valuable. It should not make the institution harder to challenge.

These are normative commitments. They do not follow automatically from an adoption survey. My reason for defending them is that AI changes who can act at scale, while the people affected may have little control over the deployment. Counting accounts misses that relationship.

For a consequential deployment, publish what changed, who benefits, who does the new checking work and how an affected person can challenge the result. Then specify what would trigger reconsideration: a material capability change, a failure pattern or evidence that the promised benefit has not appeared. A stable operating commitment with explicit review points gives people something firmer than a permanent instruction to keep up.

The frontier's clock will continue to matter whenever new capabilities alter what can be attempted. Society's clock matters because useful, legitimate arrangements cannot simply be downloaded with the model. The task is to connect them: give people the time, resources and authority to turn repeated technical change into durable improvements. Otherwise the frontier can move farther into the possible while too many people remain occupied with adapting to its previous arrival.

## Sources and method

This is a targeted synthesis of public primary sources checked through October 2, 2026, not a systematic review or a new empirical study. The newest dated statistical release used is Census BTOS, September 24, 2026. Publication dates and observation periods are separated above; the September NBER revision also includes software-marketplace observations through August 2026.

All four figures reproduce structured source values, not image-pixel estimates. Figure 1 uses METR's TH1.1 estimates and intervals, excluding older TH1.0 records and the one estimate above its stated reliable range. Release dates locate models historically; estimates are not necessarily those first published on those dates. Gallup measures employee-reported AI use, Eurostat broad enterprise AI use and Pew adult attitudes. No capability and adoption measures are combined, normalized to a common scale or extrapolated.

The [Census workbook](https://www.census.gov/hfp/btos/downloads/National.xlsx) supplies the exact question and collection/reference dates. [Eurostat's enterprise workbook](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/images/b/bf/2025_Enterprises_using_AI_tables_and_graphs.xlsx), Figure 1, supplies the size comparison. [Gallup's indicator methodology](https://www.gallup.com/699797/indicator-artificial-intelligence.aspx) defines the overlapping frequency categories. [Pew's published chart tables](https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2026/09/16/democrats-are-now-more-worried-than-republicans-about-ai-and-its-impact-on-jobs/) supply the attitude values.

The NBER studies are working papers unless a journal publication is identified. Capability gains, adoption differences and reported attitudes are directly evidenced; the moving-target mechanism and its consequences for shared expectations and agency are synthesis. Neither a quantified global lag nor a continuously widening aggregate gap is established. The two clocks are an explanatory distinction, not a claim of a measured second derivative or a universal speed of social change.
